source.title: LoRA-MGPO: Mitigating Double Descent in Low-Rank Adaptation via Momentum-Guided Perturbation Optimization
source.authors: Yu-Peng Chang; Chen-Lu Guo; Yi Chang; Yuan Wu

page_placements.theme: Non-monotone training or optimization quantities are distinct from held-out risk

record.tranche_reason: The study develops a training method intended to mitigate double descent in LoRA and reports training-loss curves, but it does not measure the test-error curves named in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The reported rank- and learning-rate-dependent training-loss curves are related to the study's LoRA instability finding, but training loss is not the test error measured by V1 or V2. The benchmark scores compare fine-tuning methods and do not test any listed double-descent version.
record.test_reason: The study's 'double descent' is a transient rise in training loss over steps during LoRA fine-tuning of LLaMA-2-7B. The claim is about test error versus size, epochs or samples. No test-error curve across model size, epochs or sample count is reported. The remaining results compare the authors' method (LoRA-MGPO) with baselines on benchmarks, so the study borrows the term rather than testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors use 'double descent' to mean a transient divergence in training loss that worsens with LoRA rank. They conclude that LoRA-MGPO removes it, giving smoother, more stable convergence and better benchmark scores than LoRA and other PEFT methods.
record.recipe_differences: The study tests momentum-guided perturbation and adaptive normalization during LoRA fine-tuning, not the original sources' test-error measurements across model size, training time, or sample size.
record.method_sensitivity: The training-loss trajectory varies with LoRA rank and learning rate; the authors report greater standard-LoRA instability at higher ranks and oscillations at higher learning rates.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard LoRA on LLaMA-2-7B/MetaMathQA shows a transient rebound in training loss. The text says it grows more severe with rank and is sharp at r=128. The authors' method removes it.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In LoRA fine-tuning, training loss shows transient divergence that worsens with adapter rank; this is distinct from test-error double descent.

fits_no_version.finding: At rank 128, higher learning rates cause training-loss oscillations in standard LoRA, while LoRA-MGPO stays stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LoRA training-loss instability grows with learning rate.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
record.problems: The relevant rank and learning-rate evidence is presented in plots without numeric loss values or uncertainty estimates. The study reports training loss rather than the test-error curves in the claim, and does not test sample-size effects or interpolation thresholds.

untested.parts: Test error versus model size or capacity near interpolation. Table 2 gives benchmark scores at LoRA ranks 8, 32 and 128 only for LoRA-GA and LoRA-MGPO; there is no vanilla LoRA rank sweep and no interpolation threshold.
Test error over epochs. Only training loss over steps is plotted.
Risk past interpolation across model classes.
Label noise, multiple peaks, and optimal regularization.

missing.what: Figure 1 training-loss curves for Full FT and LoRA at r=32/64/128. The text says Full FT shows 'even more severe double descent'; this is training loss, so it belongs with the fits_no_version findings.

record.verdict_notes: The study names a training-loss rebound 'double descent' and cites Nakkiran et al. and Belkin et al., but never measures test error against capacity, epochs or samples. Table 2's rank 8/32/128 scores cover only LoRA-GA and LoRA-MGPO, roughly increasing, and are comparisons of the study's own method. Relation could also reasonably be 'discusses' (T6).

versions.untested_parts: Test error as model size grows, including a peak near the training-set interpolation threshold.
Test error over training epochs; the study plots training loss over steps instead.
Whether increasing training-set size near interpolation raises test error.
Risk curves across model classes as capacity passes the interpolation point.
Whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
The role of label noise or variance, multiple peaks, and disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Whether measuring complexity by an effective parameter count turns second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
